description: We are siblings from Dushanbe: Shukrona is first-year dentistry student at tajik state medical university and Muhammadjon is second year student at MDIS Dushanbe and works as an AI engineer. We are interested in turning open satellite data into to that ordinary peaople can understand and use, and we want to build a clear, interactive fire calendar that shows when and where the risk is highest
summary:
Burning Calendar is a web app that puts two decades of NASA FIRMS fire hotspots on one scale. MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) count fire differently, so their records can't be compared directly.
We count one unit, a 1 km cell with fire on a given day. MODIS is then rescaled to VIIRS on the years both flew, and NOAA-20/21 carry the series past Suomi NPP. On months held out of the fit, the error drops from 71% to 10%. Region by region it is 17–19%. We show openly that a ratio borrowed from another region fails.
Users get a burning calendar from 2000 to now. They can draw an area or pick a country, compare the current month with its historical normal, see which countries are unusual right now, compare two places or times, and download hotspots as CSV.
It matters because Terra and Aqua are nearing end of life, and emergency managers need a consistent record that survives the sensor handover. Only Central Asia, Europe and South Asia are loaded so far, because of slow internet in Dushanbe. The pipeline is designed to extend to the other seven regions with one download command per region.
details:
Project Details
What it does. Burning Calendar is a web app that puts MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots (2000 to now) on one scale, so the sensor of origin stops mattering. We count one unit, a 1 km cell with fire on a day. MODIS is rescaled to VIIRS on the years both flew, and NOAA-20/21 continue the series after Suomi NPP. Users get a burning calendar (months × years), a hex map, and a headline comparing the chosen month with its own historical normal. They can draw a box or shape, pick a country, and see which countries are unusual right now. They can also compare two places or times and download hotspots (CSV) and the monthly series. On held-out months the error drops from 71% to 10% in total. Per region it is 17–19%, and we show where a borrowed ratio fails (33–38% error).
Benefits and impact. Emergency managers, scientists and land managers get a consistent record that survives the end of Terra and Aqua. They can see in seconds whether this month is normal for their area.
Tools. Python (pandas, numpy only) for the pipeline; D3 and plain JavaScript for the site; Docker; GitHub Pages and Actions; unit tests and CI; ffmpeg and headless Firefox for the screenshots and demo. We used Claude Code for coding.
Creative. The story page doubles as the presentation. Results are validated region by region and the weak spots are shown openly. It also has a "most above normal" list and shareable links.
Factors considered. Counting unit; static sources such as gas flares masked in near-real-time data; the incomplete current month, compared with a pro-rated normal; Terra-only months are least certain; and a slow-connection loader. Only Central Asia, Europe and South Asia are loaded so far, because of slow internet in Dushanbe. The pipeline can add the other seven regions.
